description: We are a team of young software development enthusiasts that excel in design, Ux, and vibecoding. If you are very ambitious and loves brainstorming, join us!
summary:
In 1930 Clyde Tombaugh, 24 and without a degree, found Pluto by blinking two photographs of the sky until a dot jumped. NASA's SPHEREx now photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours, again and again: over a million public images. The bottleneck is no longer data, it is people: about 12,000 professional astronomers for hundreds of millions of sources, any of which could hide something new. And public is not accessible: opening one image takes code and a computer.

Halo is a free web app that lets anyone join the search, on any phone, with no install and no login. It has two views. The SPHEREx viewer plays the real images of any spot on different dates (blink, slide, difference). The 3D map holds the 249,000 Gaia stars around the Sun: pick any star to see what is known about it, its path, and where it was and will be over 100,000 years.

The loop is look, analyse, register. The analyzer measures what moved or changed brightness, cross-matches Gaia and SIMBAD, and a machine-learning model we trained reads each source's spectrum. It answers in plain words: is it real, is it already known, is it a new-planet candidate? A candidate gets a name and is stored with its dates and original images, ready for astronomers to review. On the five challenge targets it finds all five.

We did not find Planet X. We made it possible for anyone to look.
details:
The problem

In 1930 Clyde Tombaugh, a 24-year-old from a farm with no degree, found Pluto by alternating two photographs of the sky until a dot jumped. He was looking for Planet X. The method is still the same; the scale changed. NASA's SPHEREx photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours, again and again. Its first data release alone has over a million images (76.9 TB), all public.

Today the search is limited by people, not by data, and that is true everywhere in the world:

  • Too few experts for too many candidates. SPHEREx measures hundreds of millions of stars and galaxies, and every one that moves or changes brightness is a candidate somebody has to check. The International Astronomical Union has about 12,000 professional astronomers.
  • Public is not accessible. Opening one SPHEREx image takes programming and a computer, while 4.7 billion people use mobile internet and, in low- and middle-income countries, the phone is the main and often the only way online: 84% of broadband connections (GSMA, 2025).
  • The will to help is there. 62% of people worldwide want to learn more about science (72% in low-income countries), yet only 43% feel they know some or a lot about it (Wellcome Global Monitor).

There is too much sky for too few scientists, and the people who could help are left outside.

What it does, in 30 seconds

Halo lets anyone hunt for what changed in NASA SPHEREx's infrared sky, on a phone, with no install and no login. The loop is look → analyse → register.

  • Two views. The SPHEREx viewer (the real infrared sky in 102 colours) and a 3D map of the 248,560 Gaia stars around the Sun.
  • Compare what changed. At any spot, real images from different dates: blink, slide (no flashing) or difference.
  • Analyse with one button. Halo measures what moved or changed brightness, checks Gaia and SIMBAD, and a machine-learning model we trained reads each source's spectrum. The answer comes in plain words: is it real, is it known, is it a new-planet candidate?
  • Follow any star. In 3D, pick a star to see what is known about it, its path, and where it was and will be across ±100,000 years.
  • Register a candidate. Mark a dot, name it, and it is stored with its dates and original images, ready for astronomers to review.
  • Made for everyone. Plain language, large buttons, English and Portuguese. Point the phone at the sky and it becomes a window (gyroscope).

What it does, in full

  1. Home. NASA's SPHEREx and Voyager 3D models (NASA Eyes on the Solar System) lead to the two views, with plain-language docs below. English by default, Portuguese in one tap.
  2. SPHEREx viewer. The full DR1 all-sky cube (102 bands, 0.75–5 µm) on an interactive sky: Gaia's colour sky from far away, SPHEREx infrared up close. Tap any object to know what it is: planets, asteroids and comets come from JPL, stars from Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD. On a phone, "Move with your phone" uses the gyroscope: turn and tilt, and the sky follows.
  3. Compare what changed. "The 5 challenge targets" open real SPHEREx images in an eyepiece, and "See what changed here" does the same at any spot. Three modes: Blink, Slide (a curtain, for people who should not watch flashing images) and Difference. Each date says how many exposures it stacks ("Aug 2025 · 23 photos").
  4. AI analyzer. One button reads every SPHEREx Level 2 exposure of the area and marks what it found on the images: planet candidate, mover, variable. It opens with the answer the challenge asks, whether a new-planet candidate was found. "Full analysis" shows the proof checklist of each finding and what is already known there (exoplanets, Solar System bodies on those dates, SIMBAD). For each source, our machine-learning model says what it looks like (star, cool star or galaxy) from its SPHEREx spectrum alone.
  5. Mark and register. A loupe plays a close-up through all exposures. Tap a dot and Halo says what it is: slow mover, appeared, too fast, already there, known, or artefact. An unexplained dot can be named and registered: it gets an ID and is stored as "under review" with its position, dates, original exposures and checklist.
  6. 3D map of the neighbourhood. The 248,560 Gaia DR3 stars within 100 parsecs (326 light-years), plus bright stars from SIMBAD and planet hosts from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.
    • Pick any star: its distance, what is known about it (a Gaia number only, a proper name, confirmed planets, a challenge target, infrared only) and a button to fly there.
    • Time: every star moves across ±100,000 years, and the chosen star draws its path (past in blue, future in amber). Barnard's Star visibly heads towards the Sun.
    • Never lost: a scale bar in light-years that follows the zoom, distance rings, and an arrow back to the Sun.
  7. Made for everyone, from children to grandparents. 48 px buttons with written names, 14 px labels on a dark backing, a 3-step intro, a short star card first with the technical data folded away, screen-reader announcements, and a no-flash alternative to blink.

How it works

The hard part was making 76.9 TB of NASA data feel instant on a phone. Six decisions did it:

  • Bytes, not files. Each SPHEREx image is a FITS file of about 65 MB. The back end reads only the image rows, flags and wavelength table it needs, straight from NASA's public S3 bucket with HTTP Range requests: about 40 MB per area, out of 76.9 TB.
  • Our own index of the archive. IRSA's search service returned errors for hours during the hackathon, so we indexed the headers of all 1.18 million DR1 files ourselves (about 90 MB). Finding the exposures of any spot now takes about 8 ms and depends on no external service. Checked against 193 saved searches: 54,410 of 54,410 images.
  • The time was waiting, not computing. We measured a new area: 3 s of processing in 200 s. Asking the faster catalogue mirror first, sharing identical requests and reading smaller headers cut it to about 20 s, with the same result.
  • Sky tiles served once. A sky tile takes about 0.7 s from IRSA. Ours pass through a server cache that also fills the gaps of DR1 and answers in 1–3 ms. A blurred local preview sits underneath, so the sky is never black.
  • Draw only when something changes. Both the sky and the 3D map stop drawing when nothing moves (0 frames while idle), which saves battery on a phone.
  • A stellar neighbourhood in 2.2 MB. The 3D map packs each star in 9 bytes (position, brightness, colour, flags). Star motion runs on the graphics card (position + velocity × time), so sliding 100,000 years costs the processor nothing: 60 frames per second on integrated graphics. The 3D engine (three.js, about 150 KB) loads only when the map opens.

The science, step by step:

  • groups exposures into visits and keeps the same wavelengths in every visit (SPHEREx's filter varies across the detector, so mixing would fake brightness changes);
  • reprojects them onto a common 6.15″/px grid;
  • rejects cosmic rays with the dichroic twin detector;
  • fits each source's motion, with errors calibrated on stars Gaia says are still;
  • compares brightness at the same wavelength and detector;
  • searches 3.8–5 µm alone for cold objects next to stars;
  • links single-epoch detections into asteroid tracks;
  • searches for slow, distant movers (Planet X) by shift-and-stack along the parallax path of 30 AU to infinity, with the opposite direction as a negative control.

Verdict: everything is cross-matched with Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, SkyBoT, 2MASS and AllWISE, and labelled confirmed, candidate or suspect, with the reasons in plain language. The machine-learning model adds its opinion on the type of each source.

Results and validation

On the five challenge targets (DR1, 6′ field, 24–42 exposures each):

  • Barnard's Star: moving, confirmed, 12.1 ± 1.2″/yr (Gaia: 10.39″/yr).
  • Epsilon Indi B: moving, confirmed, 4.2 ± 0.4″/yr at 120° (catalogue 4.68″/yr at 123°).
  • WISE 0855: moving, candidate, 8.8 ± 0.8″/yr, seen only at 3.8–5 µm and with no Gaia match (catalogue 8.15″/yr).
  • R Draconis: variable, confirmed, 92% between visits (a Mira variable).
  • RW Aurigae: variable, suspect, 20%; it saturates the detector (a T Tauri star).

Accuracy test: we ran the analysis on the 5 targets and 4 empty neighbouring fields each (25 fields, 662 sources). It found the 5 targets, 2 variables SIMBAD already lists, and nothing else. An earlier version flagged about one false mover per field.

The machine-learning model (what kind of object is this?):

  • Input: only the SPHEREx spectrum of the source, in 12 bands (two per detector), so it works exactly where no catalogue exists.
  • Training: 979 sources from 161 sky areas, labelled by independent evidence (Gaia proper motion, SIMBAD types, WISE colours, extended shape). Gradient boosting, scikit-learn.
  • Validation by sky area (5 folds, no area in both training and test): 91% accuracy. F1 score: star 0.95, galaxy 0.86, cool star 0.69. On the 160 sources labelled by SIMBAD: 90%.
  • Limits we state: cool stars are the weakest class (94 examples), and young stars and quasars were left out for lack of examples. The model gives an opinion on the type; detection is always the measured pipeline.

Speed, measured:

  • New area analysed in about 20 s (it was 200 s); the five targets open from saved results.
  • 3D map: 60 frames per second on integrated graphics, 0 frames while idle.
  • Sky tiles: 1–3 ms from our cache, against about 0.7 s from the source.

Benefits and intended impact

Halo's core value is to democratise both the access to this data and the analysis itself: anyone can look, test a dot and register a candidate, following one guided path.

It already works elsewhere: in May 2026 NASA announced that Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 volunteers doubled the number of known brown dwarfs, with WISE images; 61 of the paper's 75 authors are volunteers. Halo brings that model to NASA's newest infrared survey, on a phone. It serves a whole chain:

  • Curious people and students see a real change in the sky in one minute (Barnard's Star moving: Tombaugh needed almost a year to see a dot jump; here it takes ten seconds).
  • Teachers get links that reopen the exact case, ready for a class.
  • Citizen hunters get triage tools that answer "is it real?" for every change.
  • Researchers receive a short list of candidates with every piece of evidence (position, dates, original exposures, wavelengths, measurements) instead of hundreds of millions of points.
  • It is free, has no login to explore, runs on phones, and works in English and Portuguese.

What is creative

In the science:

  • Wavelength-matched comparison for a survey whose filter changes across the detector.
  • Reading only the needed bytes of each FITS file straight from S3, and an own index of NASA's archive, so the app keeps working when the search service is down.
  • A 3D map that explains the science: proper motion depends on distance, so the movers in SPHEREx are our neighbours. And WISE 0855, 2.3 pc away, is not in Gaia: only infrared surveys like SPHEREx can find it.

In the interface:

  • Optical glass lit by the real Sun. Every panel is a piece of thick glass floating over the live sky, and the single light that shines on all of them comes from where the Sun is today among the stars. It turns slowly as the sky moves.
  • The eyepiece. Comparing dates happens inside a telescope eyepiece over the sky, not on another page, and the same eyepiece runs the analyzer. One path from curiosity to candidate.
  • The phone as a window. With the gyroscope on, turning and tilting the phone moves the sky.
  • A 3D map light enough for any phone: 248,560 stars at 60 frames per second, with a scale bar in light-years, distance rings, time travel and the path of any star.
  • A "no-flash" Slide mode as an accessible alternative to blink.
  • Plain verdicts: the answer first (was a new-planet candidate found or not), the proof one tap away, and always "candidate", never "discovery".

Factors we considered and limitations

  • Honesty: Halo says "candidate", never "discovery". One SPHEREx exposure reaches about magnitude 17 AB, while the predicted Planet Nine is far fainter (V 22–24), so Halo will not find Planet X alone. What it does is turn a sky of changes into a short, checked list.
  • Known pitfalls we handle: blended sources in crowded fields imitate motion; saturated stars carry TRANSIENT flags in their core; masking the OUTLIER flag would erase asteroids; the dichroic frames 50 and 51 are blank.
  • IRSA is slow and unstable, so we retry and cache every call, keep 1–2 requests at a time, and ship the five test targets precomputed.
  • Accessibility: no information by colour alone (shapes and words too), a no-flash alternative to blink, keyboard operable, large touch targets (48 px), plain language first, page zoom allowed, and reduced-motion respected.

Next steps

  • Review of each candidate by several people, with votes weighted by how each reviewer does on known objects.
  • Measure how faint Halo can see by planting fake moving objects in the real images.
  • A pilot with schools and astronomy clubs.

We did not find Planet X. We made it possible for anyone to look. Tombaugh needed an observatory; today a phone is enough.

Tools

  • Front end: React, TypeScript, Vite, Aladin Lite v3 (WebGL), three.js for the 3D map.
  • Back end: Python and FastAPI, with Astropy, reproject, photutils, SciPy, NumPy and scikit-learn.
  • Data access: HTTP Range reads from AWS S3; IRSA SIA and TAP services; HiPS tiles cached on our server.

Use of AI tools

  • In the process: we used an AI coding assistant (Anthropic's Claude) to help write, review and debug code and to edit documentation and translations. Every change was directed, reviewed and tested by the team, and every scientific result was checked against catalogues (Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, JPL) and our 25-field accuracy test.
  • In the product: the "AI analyzer" button runs our measured time-domain pipeline (position fits, brightness comparison, catalogue cross-matches), which is not a language model and does not guess. Inside it, a small classifier we trained ourselves (scikit-learn, gradient boosting on 979 sources from 161 sky areas, 91% accuracy in area-wise cross-validation) gives an opinion ("star, cool star or galaxy") from a source's SPHEREx spectrum alone. It is shown as an opinion, never as a verdict.
  • What is not AI: no images, data or results in Halo are AI-generated, and no AI output carries NASA branding. Every image is real SPHEREx data, and every catalogue value comes from its archive.

References

  • Wellcome Global Monitor 2018 (Gallup): 62% of people worldwide interested in learning more about science; 43% say they know some or a lot.
  • GSMA, The State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2025: 4.7 billion mobile internet users; mobile is 84% of broadband connections in low- and middle-income countries.
  • International Astronomical Union, individual membership (about 11,500–13,700 professional astronomers, depending on the year counted).
  • NASA/JPL, SPHEREx mission: more than 450 million galaxies and more than 100 million stars to be measured; DR1 at IRSA has 1,179,406 images (76.9 TB).
  • NASA Science, "NASA Volunteers Double Known Population of Brown Dwarfs", May 2026.

Team

Team Sonder (Belo Horizonte, Brazil): Vinicius Henrique Dutra Goddard (Halo interface, analysis drawer, mobile layout, deployment fixes), Henrique Silverio Nahim (3D neighbourhood, object panel, catalogues, performance, submission), Matheus Fagundes (time-domain science, Planet X search, candidate submission, S3 index, deployment).
